video.title: Exploring a dataset: A routine for any table
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Amina Bello - primary teacher, Nigeria (main character)
Narrator - the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.narration: The ministry sent us a table: attendance and marks for every class, for a whole year. My teachers asked: where do we even start? We needed a routine.
Today: a five-question routine for exploring any table of data.
First, what is in it? Count the rows and columns. What is one row: a pupil, a class or a day? Which columns are numbers, and which are categories?
Second, the shape. Draw a histogram of each number column. Is it a hill, or does it have a long tail?
Third, the centre and the spread. Give the median and the range for skewed columns, and the mean and the standard deviation for symmetric ones.
Fourth, gaps and oddities. Look for missing values, outliers and impossible numbers, like a class with one hundred and twenty percent attendance.
Fifth, groups and relationships. Compare boys and girls, morning and afternoon, or villages. Draw a scatter plot of attendance and marks. Then ask the next question.
Quick check! One class shows one hundred and twenty percent attendance. Which step of the routine catches this?
Gaps and oddities. Attendance can't pass one hundred percent, so something went wrong, maybe pupils counted twice. Fix or flag it before you compare classes.
Then write three findings, each with evidence. For example: attendance is lowest in the rainy months, with a median of eighty percent in July. A finding needs a number and where it came from.
Your turn. Which is the better finding: attendance is bad, or attendance falls to a median of eighty percent in July?
The second one: it has a number and a time. Remember the routine: what is in it, shape, centre and spread, gaps and oddities, groups and relationships. Then write findings with evidence.
Try it in class tomorrow: give groups a small school table and the five questions on a card. Each group writes three findings with evidence and one next question.

checkpoints.prompt: A class shows 120% attendance. Which step of the routine catches this?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: impossible values are oddities to fix or flag before comparing.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: an impossible number is an oddity. Catch it before you compare classes.

options.text: Attendance falls to a median of 80% in July

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: a good finding has a number, a time and a source.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: “bad” is an opinion. A finding needs a number from the data.
